summary: The build can start: required MCP servers (documentdb and learn) and the DocumentDB agent skills are installed, Python + pip are present, and the run environment gives a reachable cluster (DOCUMENTDB_URI) and the required database name. Several cold answers were wrong or described neighbouring products (Cosmos DB, Amazon DocumentDB, or older naming). These mistakes are fixable; the builder must follow the DocumentDB skill guidance (resource type = Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters, use the DocumentDB CLI/group or az resource create against the mongoClusters resource type, use mongodb+srv style connection strings returned by the portal/gateway, compute-tier (vCore) billing, Entra authentication support, native vector and $search features, and supported change streams). Missing developer conveniences (mongosh) and a couple of minor facts (exact Beanie/Motor pin matrix) remain open but are not blocking.
summary_points: Ready to build: documentdb MCP server and the DocumentDB agent skills are installed and available; python and pip are present and DOCUMENTDB_URI is the intended runtime source for the connection string.

Major cold-answer confusions mainly came from mixing up Azure DocumentDB with older Cosmos DB 'databaseAccounts' and with Amazon DocumentDB — correct facts are in the DocumentDB skills and Learn docs (resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters, CLI group includes az documentdb / az cosmosdb mongocluster or az resource create against mongoClusters).

Key runtime facts to apply: use MongoDB drivers (Motor + Beanie) with the Mongo-style URI from DOCUMENTDB_URI, prefer mongodb+srv SRV URI returned by the service, set retryWrites=false, and tune client settings via the documentdb-driver and documentdb-connection guidance.

Change streams, native vector indexes (DiskANN/HNSW/IVF via cosmosSearch), and native full-text $search are supported by Azure DocumentDB and have DocumentDB-specific commands; using Cosmos DB docs or older pages would break the sample.

Developer tooling gaps: mongosh is not on PATH (use the documentdb MCP server tools or install mongosh), and exact Beanie/Motor version compatibility for the target wire protocol needs confirmation before pinning requirements.
No blocker-level missing tools were detected; build proceeds with minor workarounds and a short checklist for the builder.

tools.name: documentdb (MCP server)
tools.needed_for: Inspecting the live cluster (list databases, collections, create indexes, run aggregation/explain) and verifying what the sample creates.
tools.detail: documentdb MCP server present in inventory with 18 data-plane tools (list, aggregate, create_index, explain, etc.).
tools.impact_if_missing: Without it the agent cannot inspect the cluster programmatically to verify index creation, run explain plans, or sample documents; developer would need manual portal steps.
tools.workaround: Use the Azure portal for manual inspection and the 'az resource' commands, or install the DocumentDB MCP server (add entry documentdb to mcp.json).

tools.name: learn (Microsoft Learn MCP server)
tools.needed_for: Authoritative product docs and examples used to ground cold answers and choose correct APIs/commands.
tools.detail: Learn MCP server available; used to fetch Microsoft Learn pages for resource types, CLI guidance, change-stream docs, and feature lists.
tools.impact_if_missing: Without it the agent must rely on installed skills only and cannot fetch the canonical Microsoft docs during verification.
tools.workaround: Rely on the installed DocumentDB skills (they include references) and local copies of docs; install learn MCP server if web docs are required.

tools.name: python
tools.needed_for: Build and run the async Python Beanie service, run seed scripts, tests, and the change-stream consumer.
tools.impact_if_missing: Can't run or package the sample code or unit/integration tests.
tools.workaround: Install Python or run inside a provided container where Python is available.

tools.name: pip
tools.detail: pip available via environment Python (virtualenv per run environment).
tools.workaround: Use system package manager or ensure virtualenv provides pip.

tools.name: az (Azure CLI)
tools.needed_for: Inspecting subscription/resource-group context, reading resource provider registration and (optionally) running az resource create if infra steps are needed or to query cluster resource metadata.
tools.impact_if_missing: You could not confirm subscription/permissions or register the Microsoft.DocumentDB provider from the CLI; manual portal steps would be required.
tools.workaround: Use the Azure portal; the sample does not require provisioning since run environment already gives a cluster.

tools.name: docker
tools.needed_for: Optional: run the local DocumentDB Gateway container for offline integration testing (gateway listens on port 10260).
tools.detail: Docker present; but skill_md says no local gateway is running at the moment.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run a local gateway container for integration tests; will have to run against the live cluster.
tools.workaround: Run tests against the live cluster (DOCUMENTDB_URI) as the run environment instructs.

tools.name: mongosh
tools.needed_for: Optional developer convenience: manual connectivity checks, index inspection, and ad hoc queries using a Mongo shell.
tools.detail: mongosh not found on PATH per inventory.
tools.impact_if_missing: Developers cannot use a local mongosh REPL to debug queries; they'd use the documentdb MCP server or programmatic checks instead.
tools.workaround: Use the documentdb MCP server tools (find/aggregate/explain) or install mongosh (npm i -g mongosh or follow MongoDB docs).

accelerators_missed: DocumentDB Agent Kit (npx skills add Azure/documentdb-agent-kit) — the environment already has individual DocumentDB skills installed and the documentdb MCP server; installing the agent kit would centralize and speed new skill installs but is not required for this sample.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type for an account: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (child resources include databases and collections under that account).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB clusters are represented by the resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (the managed mongoClusters resource).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB and many legacy docs used the Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts resource for CosmosDB accounts; the cold answer described that older Cosmos DB account resource rather than the new first‑class DocumentDB mongoClusters resource type.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder tries to deploy or reference the cluster using Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts the commands and ARM/Bicep snippets will target Cosmos DB 'databaseAccounts' and not create or inspect DocumentDB mongoClusters; ARM templates/CLI calls would fail or operate on the wrong resource type.
improvements: On deployment quickstarts and the top-level README, replace references to Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts with Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters for the DocumentDB product.
Add an explicit deprecation note on Learn pages that previously used databaseAccounts for vCore MongoDB, pointing readers to mongoClusters for Azure DocumentDB.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the core CLI group az cosmosdb. Example to create an account: az cosmosdb create --name myaccount --resource-group myRG --locations regionName=eastus --kind MongoDB. This is in the main az CLI (not an extra extension).
confusions.grounded_answer: DocumentDB cluster management is available via the DocumentDB CLI command group (az documentdb mongocluster ...) and there are also az cosmosdb mongocluster subcommands; the deployment path used in the skill shows using az resource create against the resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters for scripted deployments. The CLI commands are in the Azure CLI command modules; some commands may be in preview and shipped via the DocumentDB CLI extension or built into the az CLI as command groups (az documentdb / az cosmosdb mongocluster).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described the older Cosmos DB workflows (az cosmosdb create against databaseAccounts). The new DocumentDB product exposes dedicated CLI command groups (az documentdb) and/or az resource create invocations against the mongoClusters type; some commands are in preview and historically lived under cosmosdb, causing overlap.

confusion_sources.title: Quickstart: Deploy an Azure DocumentDB cluster using Bicep

confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb create / databaseAccounts-based commands could create or modify a Cosmos DB account rather than a DocumentDB mongoClusters resource; the provisioning flow or returned connection strings will not match the cluster the sample is intended to use.
improvements: Add a short CLI guidance note in the agent kit and top-level README: to manage DocumentDB clusters prefer 'az documentdb mongocluster' or 'az resource create' with resource-type 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters' and include the Learn CLI pages as examples.
Document when az cosmosdb subcommands still apply and when az documentdb should be used.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep/ARM resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. Terraform resource: azurerm_cosmosdb_account.
confusions.grounded_answer: To deploy an Azure DocumentDB cluster you should use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters in Bicep/ARM. Terraform (AzAPI or provider) examples target the equivalent mongoClusters resource (azurerm_mongo_cluster or AzAPI against Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described the older Cosmos DB account resource (databaseAccounts) and the Terraform azurerm_cosmosdb_account resource; DocumentDB uses a new resource family and terraform AzAPI or azurerm_mongo_cluster patterns that target mongoClusters.
confusions.build_risk: Using databaseAccounts in IaC will target Cosmos DB's account construct and not create the DocumentDB mongoClusters resource; deployments and automation will fail the sample's expectations.
improvements: Update sample templates and quickstarts to show main.bicep examples that reference Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and include the required apiVersion (2025-09-01 or later).
Add Terraform examples using azurerm_mongo_cluster / AzAPI that explicitly target mongoClusters.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&authSource=admin&retryWrites=false (TLS/SSL must be enabled).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB provides a Mongo-style connection string commonly in SRV form. Example returned by the service: mongodb+srv://<user>:<password>@<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?tls=true&authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256&retryWrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000. Use the service-provided connection string (SRV preferred); include TLS (tls=true), authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256 and retryWrites=false.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Deploy an Azure DocumentDB cluster using Bicep

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used the older Cosmos DB Mongo connection pattern (*.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255) rather than the DocumentDB cluster SRV-style hostname (cluster.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com) and omitted service-recommended authMechanism and SRV scheme.
confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong hostname/port or leaving retryWrites at default can cause connection failures or driver errors. If the builder hardcodes port 10255 and the cluster returns an SRV URI, connection will fail or behave unpredictably.
improvements: In the sample README and connection helper code, instruct the builder to read the service-provided connection string from DOCUMENTDB_URI and to avoid hardcoding host suffixes/ports.
Document the required query options in the README: retryWrites=false and authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256 (and prefer mongodb+srv form when provided).

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Azure Cosmos DB bills by Request Units (RUs) when using provisioned throughput; it also offers a serverless option. There is not a vCore-based billing model for the classic DocumentDB/Cosmos accounts.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (the managed MongoDB-compatible service) uses compute tiers (M10..M200, vCore-like tiers such as M30 as the production default) and storage sizing per shard; pricing is compute (tier) + storage rather than Cosmos DB RU billing. The service offers a free tier cluster for dev. (Do not assume RU-based billing for DocumentDB clusters.)
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described Cosmos DB's RU-based model; DocumentDB's vCore/compute-tier billing model is different and was previously introduced as the 'vCore' style offering replacing RU billing for that product family in some modes.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes RU quotas and chooses indexes/aggregation patterns accordingly, they may under- or oversize the cluster. Cost estimates and guidance in README would be incorrect.
improvements: Add an explicit billing note in the sample README: DocumentDB uses compute-tier (M10..M200) + storage, not Cosmos DB RU/s, and link to the official pricing page.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: The MongoDB API for Cosmos DB uses MongoDB SCRAM-style username/password authentication. Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) is not supported as a direct MongoDB driver authentication mechanism; drivers authenticate with the MongoDB URI and credentials.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports both native (SCRAM) authentication and Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) / RBAC for cluster access; the service supports Entra ID modes and managed identities for service-to-service scenarios. The az CLI and cluster APIs expose auth modes (e.g., --auth-allowed-modes includes MicrosoftEntraID). Follow documentdb-security guidance for using Entra RBAC and Key Vault-backed secrets for credentials.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB Mongo API accounts historically had fewer Entra/managed-identity options and documentation often said only SCRAM credentials were used; DocumentDB includes Entra ID and RBAC patterns for the managed service, so the cold answer reflects older product constraints.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes Azure AD cannot be used, they may hardcode long-lived keys or primary passwords in dev scripts rather than using managed identities or Key Vault references, increasing security risk.
improvements: Add a short authentication section in the sample README explaining that DocumentDB supports SCRAM credentials and Microsoft Entra ID / managed identities, and link to documentdb-security.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the standard MongoDB drivers for your language (e.g. pymongo or motor for Python async). There is no separate MongoDB-specific service SDK for DocumentDB; the MongoDB-compatible endpoints are consumed via normal MongoDB drivers. For higher-level ODM in Python, use Motor + Beanie (Beanie runs on top of Motor/pymongo).
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use the standard MongoDB drivers (Motor for async Python) and an ODM like Beanie on top of Motor for the async Python sample. DocumentDB is MongoDB-wire-compatible, so drivers and ODMs that target the Mongo wire protocol work. Follow documentdb-driver guidance for client singleton patterns and connection options.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: n/a
confusions.build_risk: None — this is the correct guidance.

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: There is no native vector-indexing feature in the classic Cosmos DB MongoDB API; you cannot create HNSW/DiskANN/IVF vector indexes with a MongoDB createIndex call.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB includes native vector-index support (index types such as DiskANN, HNSW, and IVF) exposed through the service's `createSearchIndexes` / `cosmosSearch` mechanics and vector index creation commands described in the documentdb-vector-search guidance; you can create vector indexes and query them via the $search aggregation stage + cosmosSearch operator.

grounding_links.title: Compare Azure DocumentDB to MongoDB Atlas

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described classic Cosmos DB Mongo API (which historically lacked first-class vector indexes) or older guidance; DocumentDB (the new product) includes first-class vector index support and specific index types.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes vector search isn't available they may build an external vector pipeline or avoid demonstrating combined lexical+vector queries; they'd miss a natural built-in capability.
improvements: Document in the sample README that DocumentDB supports vector indexes (DiskANN/HNSW/IVF) and link to the vector index creation example from the vector-search skill.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Full-text and hybrid (semantic) search are done by integrating Cosmos DB with Azure Cognitive Search or by exporting documents to a search index; Cosmos DB does not provide a feature-equivalent of MongoDB Atlas Search inside the Mongo API.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB exposes native full-text search via createSearchIndexes and the $search aggregation stage (BM25 scoring, analyzers), and supports hybrid search (BM25 + vector) using the same search primitives; the documentdb-full-text-search skill documents the createSearchIndexes command and $search usage. You do not need an external Azure Cognitive Search to get DocumentDB's built-in full-text and hybrid search features.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer reflected an older pattern (Cosmos DB SQL API often integrated with Azure Cognitive Search). DocumentDB provides internal $search and createSearchIndexes primitives distinct from the external Azure Cognitive Search integration.
confusions.build_risk: Relying on an external search service complicates the sample and obfuscates built-in $search usage examples; the sample should demonstrate built-in $search and (if relevant) hybrid BM25+vector queries.
improvements: Show a minimal createSearchIndexes + $search example in the sample README and code; link to documentdb-full-text-search guidance.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically Cosmos DB's MongoDB API matched specific MongoDB server versions (3.6/4.0/4.2...). Expect limited support compared to stock MongoDB: some admin commands and server-side features are missing and historically limited or no support for multi-shard distributed transactions and MongoDB change streams.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports modern MongoDB wire protocol versions (5.0, 6.0, 7.0, 8.0) and implements wide operator coverage (documentation lists supported MQL features and any limited/unavailable administrative commands). Many commonly used features (change streams, transactions, and aggregation stages) are supported; check the compatibility tables for any specific operator or command differences. Test features against the target cluster and use the free compatibility assessment tooling for migrations.

grounding_links.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer mixed older limitations of Cosmos DB and generic cautions about any managed PaaS offering with the present DocumentDB feature set; compatibility claims must be checked per version and operator.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming missing features (e.g., no change streams) can lead the builder to implement unnecessary workarounds or avoid demonstrating server-side aggregation features that are supported.
improvements: Add a one-line compatibility note in the sample README: 'DocumentDB supports MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0–8.0; verify specific operators/stages with the compatibility page before using advanced aggregation operators.'

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: Azure provides an Azure Cosmos DB Emulator but it historically supports only the SQL (Core) API locally and not the MongoDB API. For MongoDB-compatible development you should run a local MongoDB (official docker image) for fast local iteration. The Cosmos Mongo endpoint uses port 10255 for TLS; a local Mongo image usually listens on 27017.
confusions.grounded_answer: For DocumentDB there is a local Gateway Docker image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest) that exposes the MongoDB wire protocol on port 10260 (and PostgreSQL on 9712). The DocumentDB local Gateway is the recommended local dev option; do not rely on the Cosmos DB emulator which targets the SQL (Core) API.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer mixed Cosmos DB emulator limitations with general MongoDB practice. DocumentDB provides a gateway local image listening on 10260 (not Cosmos emulator behavior).

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB Emulator limitations (SQL-only) — historical pages

confusions.build_risk: If the builder tries to run the Cosmos DB emulator expecting Mongo endpoints, local tests will fail or mislead; they should prefer the DocumentDB gateway container for proper parity.
improvements: Add a local-dev section in README recommending the DocumentDB Gateway Docker image (port 10260) and include a minimal docker-compose snippet from documentdb-local-deployment.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Cosmos DB offers a Change Feed for its containers (a service-specific change notification stream), but MongoDB-style change streams are not generally available on the Mongo API; use Cosmos DB Change Feed instead.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB-style change streams (collection.watch / Model.watch) and provides DocumentDB-specific change-stream features (resume tokens, historical checkpoints). For multishard clusters a portal preview setting may need to be toggled for some advanced scenarios. DocumentDB also documents a Change Streams page with usage examples.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described Cosmos DB's change feed (a different API) and older limitations for the Mongo API; DocumentDB supports MongoDB-style change streams and documents how to use and resume them.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes change streams are unsupported they may implement polling or convoluted websockets; instead, the sample should open a change stream with the driver and demonstrate alerts.
improvements: In the sample README show the minimal Motor/Beanie snippet to open collection.watch and include a note about the 'Change streams for multishard clusters' portal feature if the sample targets a multishard cluster.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: For DocumentDB/Cosmos DB the service-specific MCP server would be the 'documentdb' MCP server. The general Azure MCP server covers many Azure resources, but a documentdb-specific MCP is used for data-plane inspection and agent tools.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the documentdb MCP server exposes data-plane tools (query, aggregate, index management, explain). The general azure MCP server provides control-plane operations across Azure but documentdb provides the data-plane tooling agents need.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: n/a
confusions.build_risk: None — the environment includes the documentdb MCP server to run data-plane checks.

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: ‘DocumentDB’ was the original name of Microsoft's managed JSON document database service; it was later rebranded and expanded as Azure Cosmos DB. Azure Cosmos DB is Microsoft’s multi-model globally distributed database service; this is not the same as any unrelated open-source 'DocumentDB' project — Cosmos DB is a proprietary Microsoft engine.
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly wrong: the name history is confusing. The product now called 'Azure DocumentDB' (the managed MongoDB-compatible service described here) was previously available as the vCore-based 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)'. It is built on the open-source 'DocumentDB' engine (microsoft/documentdb) — the engine project is separate and open-source, and DocumentDB (the engine) can also run locally. Do not conflate the old 'DocumentDB' branding (early Cosmos DB era) with the current product naming.

grounding_links.title: Moving from another MongoDB-compatible service to Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Multiple products have used 'DocumentDB' and 'Cosmos' in overlapping ways historically (legacy Azure DocumentDB → Cosmos DB rename, the vCore offering, and now the DocumentDB managed service) which makes name-based confusion common.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses naming from older docs they may write inaccurate README text or link to the wrong deployment guides, confusing users and reviewers.
improvements: Add a short 'product name' paragraph in the repo README clarifying: 'Azure DocumentDB (this sample) is the managed MongoDB-compatible service backed by the open-source DocumentDB engine; do not confuse with Cosmos DB databaseAccounts or Amazon DocumentDB.'
Add a cross-reference in older docs or the agent kit to point to the new DocumentDB pages.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Under the MongoDB-compatible API, the underlying engine is Cosmos DB's proprietary storage and runtime that implements the MongoDB wire protocol. That means most MongoDB drivers work, but there are subtle behavioral and feature differences.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine (microsoft/documentdb) and implements the MongoDB wire protocol — drivers and application code that use standard MongoDB drivers will generally work, but there are platform-specific differences (admin commands and some operators may differ). The underlying engine being DocumentDB does not require driver changes; follow compatibility docs for operator-level differences.

grounding_links.title: Compare Azure DocumentDB to MongoDB Atlas

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumed the Cosmos DB engine implementation rather than the open-source DocumentDB engine that now power this DocumentDB product; the practical outcome (driver compatibility caveats) is similar but the attribution is wrong.
confusions.build_risk: Less severe — wrong attribution of engine doesn't break the sample, but it may mislead readers about where to look for engine-level code or open-source artifacts.
improvements: Clarify in README that DocumentDB uses the open-source DocumentDB engine and include a link to the engine repo for curious readers.

confusions.question: Which database name should this sample use?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the database named sample_healthcare_07 for everything this sample creates.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — the run environment and prompt specify using database 'sample_healthcare_07'.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: n/a
confusions.build_risk: None — follow the run environment directive.

confusions.question: How should the app obtain the cluster connection and how to instantiate an async Mongo client in Python?
confusions.cold_answer: Read the Mongo URI from environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI and pass it to Motor. Example code: AsyncIOMotorClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI']).
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: read DOCUMENTDB_URI from the environment and instantiate an AsyncMotor client (Motor) and use a process-wide singleton or per-process connect pattern recommended by documentdb-driver/documentdb-connection. Ensure driver options include tls/tlsAllowInvalidCertificates in local dev (gateway) and retryWrites=false in production URIs.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: n/a
confusions.build_risk: None if the environment variable is used securely and driver options recommended by documentdb-connection are applied.

confusions.question: Which indexes should the sample create for time-series lab results to make aggregations and change-stream/scan efficient?
confusions.cold_answer: Create a compound ascending index on (patientId, testCode, timestamp).
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct and recommended: a compound index { patientId: 1, testCode: 1, timestamp: 1 } supports partitioned ordered aggregations (setWindowFields) and efficient range queries by patient/test/time; documentdb-indexing recommends ESR ordering for equality+sort+range patterns (Equality → Sort → Range).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: n/a
confusions.build_risk: None — create the compound index before running aggregation demos.

confusions.question: How to open a real-time change stream in the app (driver code you would write)?
confusions.cold_answer: With Motor/pymongo use the collection.watch API and iterate the change stream. Example (async): change_stream = collection.watch(pipeline=None, full_document='updateLookup'); async for change in change_stream: handle(change). Note: if the Cosmos Mongo API does not support MongoDB change streams, the fallback is to use Cosmos DB Change Feed via Cosmos SDK/Azure Functions.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct for DocumentDB: the sample should use collection.watch (Motor) with fullDocument='updateLookup' and iterate asynchronously; DocumentDB supports change streams and documents resume and historical checkpoint options. If the target cluster is multishard and needs the portal preview change-streams-for-multishard feature, follow the portal guidance before running watch on multishard clusters.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The driver code is correct but the cold answer hedged with a Cosmos DB fallback; for this product the driver approach is primary and the fallback is unnecessary except for unusual legacy accounts.
confusions.build_risk: Minor: if the builder avoids change streams unnecessarily they'll miss the live-alert demo; ensure the sample uses collection.watch unless the specific cluster has a preview feature gating multishard change streams.
improvements: Add a short code snippet and a one-line note in README: 'Use Motor collection.watch; if your cluster is multishard enable the 'Change streams for multishard clusters' portal preview feature.'

confusions.question: What aggregation pipeline will compute a moving average and flag out-of-range values?
confusions.cold_answer: Use $setWindowFields partitioned by patientId and testCode to compute a moving average, then $addFields to flag extremes. Example pipeline using $setWindowFields, with a documents window [-4,0], then $addFields comparing value against refHigh/refLow.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: $setWindowFields partitioned by patientId and testCode with sortBy timestamp and an output $avg over a sliding documents window (e.g., [-N,0]) is the recommended server-side moving average approach; follow documentdb-indexing and aggregation compatibility docs to ensure the server version supports $setWindowFields. If a target cluster/protocol version lacks $setWindowFields, fallback options exist (aggregation with $group + $push and array ops or client-side rolling window).

grounding_links.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: n/a
confusions.build_risk: If $setWindowFields is not supported on a specific cluster/server-version, the aggregation will fail — verify the server version on the cluster and fall back if needed.

information_gaps.title: Beanie/Motor compatibility matrix
information_gaps.description: Exact recommended package versions (Beanie and Motor and PyMongo) that are guaranteed compatible with the DocumentDB wire protocol versions (5.0–8.0) and with Python 3.13 (inventory shows Python 3.13.13). Looked in: installed documentdb-driver skill docs and Microsoft Learn compatibility pages; none provide an explicit pinned matrix for Beanie/Motor versions.

information_gaps.title: Reference range source for demo
information_gaps.description: The sample prompt left unclear whether reference ranges and critical thresholds should be hard-coded, stored in a DB collection, or fetched from an external service. Looked in: prompt_review, sample prompt and skills — no authoritative guidance found.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Deploy and reference DocumentDB clusters using the Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters resource (CLI 'az documentdb mongocluster' or 'az resource create' with resource-type 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters'), not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts.

Read the connection string from DOCUMENTDB_URI (do not hardcode host suffix/port). Use the service-provided SRV/URI and include tls=true and authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256 and retryWrites=false (follow documentdb-connection tuning).

Use standard MongoDB async drivers (Motor) + Beanie ODM and apply the documentdb-driver singleton pattern (process-wide AsyncIOMotorClient) and connection options recommended by documentdb-connection.
Create an index { patientId: 1, testCode: 1, timestamp: 1 } before running aggregation demos and follow the ESR (Equality → Sort → Range) rule for compound index shape.

Open a change stream with Motor's collection.watch (fullDocument='updateLookup') to trigger alerts; if your target cluster is multishard follow the portal guidance to enable 'Change streams for multishard clusters' before relying on multishard resume semantics.
